utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Ierace, I see you're on your feet. I promised more or less yesterday to Mr. Piletta-Zanin that he would get 10 minutes. If there's any specific reason why you think you would be the first this morning, please explain it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: There is, Mr. President. The first witness to be called this morning is Rasid Dzonko. The exhibit list does not include a video that was taken in relation to the relevant incident, and it should. Steps are being taken to bring the video to Court. I should indicate that it has been disclosed along with all of the other videos, and its contents are similar, that is, the witness is seen to point out relevant features. I apologise for not having included it in the exhibit list, and I seek the leave of the Trial Chamber to add it to this morning's list. In other words, it is on the exhibit list, but it has not been included in the list for today. I don't know whether my friends are disadvantaged by that. As I say, it has been disclosed and the contents are the usual contents. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask you, is this a video about an incident the witness will testify about?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It is, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honour. Your Honours, Mr. President, thank you for giving us the floor. First of all, let me bid good morning to all of you. I think that these two issues can be treated at the same time. Or perhaps would you want us first to respond to the problem concerning the document? In which case, I can do it hic et nunc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Very well, I will take this opportunity and address the issue of exhibits. The Defence does not accept, and categorically so, this new way of proceedings. The Prosecution had ample opportunity to disclose within time limits this document. There is another reason for which we cannot accept this exhibit. In this trial, after you have had the problem of black boxes, I think now we are faced with the problem of blank boxes -- white boxes. I have to show you an example. This document concerns the following witness. This is what we received earlier on. We have not asked for a better copy, because the translation that we had in front of us reads literally as follows: "The remaining portion of the text is not legible." So we concluded that it was not possible to translate the remainder of the text. We received yesterday the same document, but instead of having this black box syndrome, we have a white box syndrome. We have received a more complete translation, but if I take any line as an example, first of all, I have the word "illegible"; then in the second line, four times illegible; fourth line, five times illegible. And so on and so forth. You can see it from the distance. The only thing we have is just illegible words. I don't know if, realistically speaking, we can accept that the Defence can conduct its preparations with the certificates which could not be translated and all we have is just a string of words, illegible, illegible, illegible. So that is the first issue that I wanted to raise. We are very -- once again, very categorical about the issue of both the tape and the certificate. The number is P2771.1, which is probably going to be tendered shortly by the Prosecution. The document has more words marked as illegible than the words that have actually been translated. Let me now go back to the crucial issue in respect of which I wanted you to give us some more time; namely, the issue of instructions. What we would like to obtain from the Prosecution in accordance with Rules 66 and 68 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence is the collection of significant documents which are in the possession of the Prosecution. That is, the documents concerning the headquarters of the general staff. There is a number of instructions which are indispensable for the preparation of the Defence. The first group concerns the relationship between the headquarters of the so-called Sarajevo army on one side and its brigades on the other -- I'm sorry, let me correct myself -- and its corps. So the links between the headquarters and the corps. This is the first echelon of command. The Prosecution is telling us that we are talking about a huge quantity of documents, which is not totally accurate simply because, Your Honours, this documentation exists. The Prosecution has produced these documents in another case which is currently pending before another Chamber. The references of this trial were given to the Prosecution, and this procedure is taking place within this other trial. So we don't need to envisage an expedition to Sarajevo or to any other location because the Prosecution is already in the possession of these documents and this type of information, which have all been disclosed in another case. The same goes for the second echelon of command, that is to say, the area of command between corps and brigades. That is the second level of command; the relationship between the corps and the brigades. What we wish to obtain, of course, are not specific and concrete orders, because there are no such orders in this particular case, but we need the so-called directives. It is the same term that is used in the English language. And these directives comprise a so-called global orders, the orders concerning a global strategy of the army. Why is this necessary for the Defence? It is our submission, Your Honour, that there were battles, and there was fighting going on during the relevant times, and that this fighting consisted, of course, of shelling or sniping or simply firing from fire weapons and so on and so forth. And of course, during that period of time, there was a considerable risk of mistargeting. We wish to show a number of attacks or plans of attacks on the part of the so-called Sarajevo army so that we can show that, as far as the other side is concerned, there were necessarily some defensive operations. I'm not talking about retaliation, but defensive operations. Of course, there was very often exchanges of fire involving relevant weapons. What we wish to show, Your Honours, is that these movements of troops and general orders which had to be issued by the headquarters, of course imply a certain number of transport of troops and equipment and so on and so forth. Every time when there is a transport of either troops or equipment, there is always the risk of accidents involving shooting and exchanges of fire in general. It is also important for the Defence to be able to show that there was a strategy on the part of the so-called Sarajevo army. Why? We will be able to show that such strategy existed with the use of these directives. It is not the task of the Defence, but I think that we can assist the Prosecution in trying to establish the truth, that we would like to show there was no asystematic shelling or sniping campaign throughout the relevant times. But that there were quite legitimate actions and operations which were -- which could be expected in view of the general situation and which we want to show with the assistance of these documents. So in a nutshell, we need the directives issued by the headquarters to the army in general, army corps, and then from the army corps to their respective brigades so that we can see what was exactly going on in Sarajevo during the relevant times. Of course, I am talking about the period of time between August -- September 1992 and August 1994. I don't think that it is an impossible exercise for the Prosecution because, once again, these documents have already been disclosed within the framework of another case. Thank you very much for giving us this opportunity to address the Chamber on this issue. Thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, as far as I understand Mr. Piletta-Zanin at this moment, what he essentially did is to explain why he thinks that certain materials are material for the Defence or exculpatory. Would you like to respond now or would you like to respond later today or --?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'm happy to respond now, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think I can do so briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: There is no issue between the Prosecution and the Defence in relation to those two categories of documents. I explained to the Trial Chamber last Thursday what steps we were taking to ascertain what the office of the Prosecutor holds, which is relevant to its obligations under Rule 66 (B) and Rule 68. So I don't know that we need to spend any more time on that issue. I anticipated to you last week that by the first week of April, I will be able to inform the Trial Chamber whether there are any documents we possess which are relevant and which we have not yet disclosed. That follows on the Defence informing the Office of the Prosecutor that it believes that there may be documents or that there are documents which have been tendered in another case. Mr. President, in relation to the medical report, my friend complains that the first version of the report was largely illegible. Of course, the Prosecution would have preferred to have disclosed a legible version. Steps were taken to obtain legible versions late last year. I have informed the Trial Chamber of that previously. And as a result, it seems that a more legible version was obtained and it has been disclosed. It is still not entirely legible. As can be seen, there are passages which are either entirely illegible or only partly legible. I do not understand why my friend blames the Prosecution for that. The Prosecution makes available the best copies it is able to obtain. It is as simple as that. It is not the fault of the Prosecution if there are not legible copies which are obtainable. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, as far as the disclosure of documents is concerned, I would say the army documents, you explained to us why they are material to the Defence in your view and why they might even be exculpatory. I do understand from Mr. Ierace that there is no major disagreement perhaps on that, but that he'll first do his homework, see what comes up. So I think until we have seen the results of the research of Mr. Ierace, there's no reason at this moment, although it's good to have your explanation as far as the materiality is concerned and as far as the possible exculpatory character of the evidence is concerned, to first wait and see what comes up, and then see whether that is acceptable or not in view of Rules 66 and 68. Then, the second issue of the medical documents, of course, we haven't seen them yet. As we did last time, as soon as they will be tendered, I do understand that you have objected already in advance. So I think before showing it to the witness, perhaps also keeping in mind what the testimony of the witness was until that moment, and for what probative purposes the medical record is tendered, we'll then give a decision on whether these records are admissible in evidence or not. The document you showed to us, may I assume that that's the better legible copy last been provided by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, at any rate, that is the best copy received by the Defence. I'm sure about that. Tomorrow, perhaps we will be given even better copies than the one that we already have. But I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if by that question to my friend you had in mind the copy that my friend held up which had a large area in black, that is not the most legible version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like now to have the best copy of both parties, which, Mr. Usher, would you please, so that we can compare them. And the other one as well. I'm not going to read them, I'm just going to compare them in view of...

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can hand up the original copy held by the Prosecution. I'll make that available.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have given you two examples. The clearer copy is the more recent one, and the other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, which copy did you show us from a distance? It was this one, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [In English] Both, both. That's the reason why I gave you both, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's then clear. That's the second copy is the better readable one. Mr. Ierace, it was not in my recollection, but both my colleagues say that both copies have been put in the air. So that we now see that the Defence has -- let me just compare them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I return them to the -- these are the ones that came from the Defence. This is the one that came from the Prosecution. So we now have seen the best available copy provided by the Prosecution. We'll give a decision when it comes to -- when the Prosecution will tender the document. That about the medical documents. What else did we have? Yes, the videotape is the last issue raised this morning. I do understand that the videotape has been disclosed to the Defence, but it has not been indicated to the Defence in due time that it would be played. On the other hand, I also do understand that the videotape deals with the specific incident on which the witness will testify. May I please hear from the Defence on whether they think they could cross-examine the witness even though the Prosecution has failed to give a timely indication that they would use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Not only were we taken by surprise, but also it was not the first time and probably not the last time. We will, despite that fact, demonstrate our usual flexibility in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Then I think, Mr. Ierace, having dealt with the problems, you could call your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And I express my gratitude to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll have -- yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, for the sake of clarity, I didn't mention a moment ago, though I was speaking about the documents, what was the name of the procedure that is the case in which the Prosecutor has already disclosed these documents. So let me tell you, it is the case against Mario Kordic. I think that is the name of the case. I don't have the number of the case, but I hope that this information will be sufficient to the Prosecution. This case is still pending.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I don't want to waste time, Mr. President. But it was I who informed the Defence of the name of the case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm quite sure that somewhere over the next break, you will agree on which case it was. Then, Mr. Ierace, would you please call your next witness. Let's first see whether the videolink is functioning well. Yes, I see that we have a videolink with Sarajevo. Ms. Philpott, are you able to understand us? I think I saw you giving an answer, but I didn't hear anything. Could you please speak a few words.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Sarajevo] Yes, good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was quite audible. So I think if the videolink is functioning well -- perhaps we should just give a test and say a few more words so that we know for sure that we're able to hear each other.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Sarajevo] One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Ms. Philpott. I think, Mr. Ierace, you agree that the witness can be I would say brought into the courtroom but brought within the videolink area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I call Rasid Dzonko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, for giving me the floor. I'm taking advantage of this pause in the absence of the witness actually to know in very exact terms whether Mr. Ierace can tell us the name of the witness. I'm asking this question because we have a number of documents. Sometimes he refers to him as Dzonko, sometimes Dzenko, and so on. So could Mr. Ierace tell us the exact name of the next witness. Is it Dzonko or Dzunko or what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, do you have any other persons in mind which he could be confused with, Mr. Piletta-Zanin? Because Mr. Ierace might then ask exactly how his name is spelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be a good idea for all of us if he did that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, may I expect that you'll pay proper attention to the issue just raised. Good morning, Witness. I'll not call you by your name under these specific circumstances. Good morning. You're at a great distance from us here in The Hague, and you'll testify before the Tribunal but before giving your testimony, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of this declaration will be handed out to you now by Ms. Philpott. May I invite you to make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, and only -- and nothing but the truth; the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You'll first be examined by counsel for the Prosecution. After that, you will be examined by counsel for the Defence. And whenever the Judges have any additional questions to you, they will put them to you. Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Ierace:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is your name Rasid Dzonko?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please spell your name.

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: D-Z-O-N-K-O. D-Z-O-N-K-O. R-A-S-I-D is the first name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dzonko. Were you born on the 25th of December in 1926?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1994, were you living in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your address in 1994?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: In Sarajevo, Senada Mandica Street, number 5.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you live there with in 1994?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: With my son-in-law and my daughter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that an apartment building with a number of floors?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes. It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many floors did the apartment building have?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Eight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what floor did you live?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Seven.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1994, how far was that place, approximately, from the confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Well, about 50 to 60 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the conflict in Sarajevo, were you injured?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: It happened in July, in the evening at 10.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereabouts were you when that happened?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: I was in the kitchen. We were sitting there and watching television. We were watching the World Championship, a football game.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else was in the apartment with you at that time?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Well, my three daughters. We had met there. I came and sat with them right up until my injury. My son-in-law was there and his two daughters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your wife present at that time?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: I don't have a wife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, you've told us your three daughters were present, your son-in-law, and two of your grandchildren. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did either of your other two daughters have any children?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us that you were watching television at the time that you were shot and that that was about 10.30 p.m. Whereabouts were you shot?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what part of your body did the bullet enter?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: It hit me in the back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what part of your back; the upper back, the middle back, or the lower back?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: The middle back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the entry point towards the spine or to one side?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: To one side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that your left side or your right side?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Left side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the bullet stay in your body or did it pass through your body?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: It passed through my body and exited and hit the wall, and then continued on through the door and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Through what part of your body did the bullet exit?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Here, by the stomach.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you could stand up, Mr. Dzonko, and point to the part of your body where the bullet came out. There is no need to lift up your clothes.

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. President, the witness indicates his left side, left front side, about halfway down the torso.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dzonko. You may sit down again. How big was the hole made by the bullet when it left your body?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Well, it was, I would say, 5 to 6 centimetres wide.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the bullet, after it left your body, hit the wall. Do you know what happened to the bullet after it hit the wall?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: It hit the wall, and then continued on, hitting the door, the hanging part on the door. And there was a chandelier in the cupboard that my daughter had taken down to prevent it from being damaged, but, unfortunately, the bullet passed through all that, destroyed the lighting and lodged somewhere there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any medical attention that night?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: I was taken to hospital straight away, to Kosevo, the hospital in Kosevo, and I stayed there for 13 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any treatment at any other place before you were taken to Kosevo Hospital?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any stage during your treatment did you attend Dobrinja Hospital?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: When they took me, I went to Dobrinja. That's where they bandaged my wound, and then I continued on upwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear any shooting earlier that night, that is, before you were shot?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Well, there was very little shooting. It would stop for a bit, then continue, and that was what it was like every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear any shot at about the time that you were shot?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear any shooting immediately after you were shot?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any soldiers positioned in your building at that time, that is, around the middle of 1994?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of there being any armaments or soldiers anywhere in your building on the day or evening that you were shot?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: No. We couldn't even get to the part where the soldiers were. I never actually saw them, the people who were up there, looking after their families. But I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you were only 50 metres from the front line. What part of your apartment faced the direction of the front line?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Well, actually it was the balcony, the balcony where I was hit. That is directly facing the front line. There's a building in front of us, and in between the two buildings, you -- there's -- it's open space. You can see right the way through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you understand that an investigation was carried out after you were taken from the apartment?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: People from IFOR came, and they took the bullet and then took photographs of it and examined it, but I wasn't there then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you said it was people from IFOR. Do you mean IFOR or another United Nations military organisation?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't say exactly who they were, but they came in a car, one of them stayed in the car, and that's what I learned when I was in hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you that in hospital, or how did you find out in hospital?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: When my son-in-law came to visit, he said that these people came by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, given how --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm reacting a little late. I apologise. But I see in line 12, the answer given by the witness was IFOR. I-F-O-R, IFOR. And then another line which is line 11, which is disappearing from our screens now, when I see the successive question, the next question by Mr. Ierace, which refers to another military organisation of the United Nations, another United Nations military organisation, I don't see that the witness mentioned any United Nations military organisation. And therefore, Mr. Ierace's question seems to me to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it the position of the Defence that IFOR was not a UN military organisation? I just ask to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what the witness thinks that IFOR stands for. I don't know whether he knows what IFOR stands for, the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was asking a question, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Could you please tell me whether the Defence takes the position that IFOR was not a UN military organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me consult the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer I was given is that it was an organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. The information contained in the second question doesn't make the question inadmissible. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonko, you told us that your balcony faced the direction of the front line. From your balcony, could you see the --

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- any of the area of the other side of the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes, you could see during the day. During the daytime, you could see. But we weren't there -- we had to hide, so we would hide in the other room and would only sit in the kitchen at these other times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On which side of the confrontation line did you live? In other words, which of the armed forces controlled the area where you lived?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which forces controlled that part of the other side of the confrontation line that could be seen from your balcony?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: They were the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonko, some people might say that it wasn't very sensible to live in a place that was so close to the confrontation line. Did you have the option of moving to a different area further away?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: No, I didn't have anywhere to live -- anywhere else. My son-in-law had a house there, and my daughter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonko, what was the room immediately alongside the balcony?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: The kitchen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the nature of the wall between the kitchen and the balcony? In other words, was it windows or a brick wall or what?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: It was a brick wall, but there was a door there going out onto the balcony and a window looking towards the direction from where I was wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 17th of July, 1994, did the window have any glass?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: There was glass up at the top, up until halfway down the door. But the bottom part was wooden planks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you referring to the door or a window?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: The door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the window? Did that have any glass in it?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any coverings over the window and the glass portion of the door on that evening?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes, the blinds and two blankets were put up to block the view. You couldn't see anything, but the light wasn't on anyway, just the television set was on. And we put two blankets to cover up the windows, and the blinds were down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which direction was the screen of the television facing at the time you were shot?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: It was facing me, inwards, not outwards. It was inside the room next to the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonko, shortly you will see a video on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this point, I would ask that the technical booth play the video. The Exhibit Number is P3279TT. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonko, can you see anything on the screen at the moment?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: No. I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. President, we could restart the video and ensure the screen has the image.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace. Could, perhaps, the representative of the Registry in Sarajevo confirm to us if the screen --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Sarajevo] Yes, Your Honour. We do have the video on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then please may the video be played further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "THE INVESTIGATOR ON TAPE: Mr. Dzonko, I will now give you some instructions. Please stand where you were -- where you were located when you were shot. "THE WITNESS: [Indicates] "THE INVESTIGATOR ON TAPE: Please assume the position you were in, to the best of your recollection, at the time you were shot. "THE WITNESS: [Indicates] "THE INVESTIGATOR ON TAPE: It is my understanding that there was wood on the door of this apartment at about the time that you were shot. Can you please indicate, with your hand, the level to which the wood covered the door. "THE WITNESS: [Indicates] "THE INVESTIGATOR ON TAPE: Can you please indicate, with your finger, to the best of your recollection where the bullet hole came through the door on the day that you were shot. "THE WITNESS: [Indicates] "THE INVESTIGATOR ON TAPE: Thank you. Could you please take your seat again, sir. "And finally, could you please point to the location where the television set was located on the day that you were shot. "THE WITNESS: [Indicates] "THE INVESTIGATOR ON TAPE: Thank you."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonko, did you recognise yourself in that video?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you comply with the requests of the investigator truthfully and to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the TV which appeared in the video the same one or a different one that you were watching on the night that you were shot?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: The same one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the direction in which the television was facing on the night that you were shot different or the same as it appeared in the video?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: The same as it is now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wish to show some photographs to the witness. Perhaps I could have some assistance to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The first photograph that I show to the witness is part of P3279T, photograph marked 34A.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In a moment, Mr. Dzonko, you should see a photograph on the screen in front of you. Can you tell us when you can see a photograph. Can you now see a photograph in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise yourself?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you seated in the apartment in which you lived in 1994?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the approximate position where you were seated when you were shot?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the photograph, we can see a railing on the balcony. Was that there when you were shot?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: One part was there, but the other one was destroyed because two shells had fallen on the same balcony prior to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe to us which part was there and which part was not.

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: The part that was missing was on the left side, and the other one was on the right side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to the part of the balcony that appears in this photograph, was any part of that missing -- I withdraw that. What about the parts of the balcony that can be seen in the photograph? Were they there, or any parts of that part of the balcony with a railing, on the night that you were shot?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: There's nothing there, just the wooden planks on the door. There was no glass in the bottom part of the door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to the green-painted railing which appears in the photograph, did that part of the balcony have any railing on the night that you were shot?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes, it did. What you can see here, but on the left side of the balcony, there was nothing. The part that you can see now was there at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. You will now see another photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Might photograph 9A be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the building which appears in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the apartment building in which you lived on the day or the night that you were shot?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the balcony of your apartment on the row of green-painted balconies that appears towards the centre of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: The mid portion that was destroyed, there is another balcony above.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you mean that you were on the second balcony from the top in the middle column of balconies in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the left of your balcony, as one looks at the photograph, there appear to be some three impact marks on the orange-coloured wall of the apartment block next door. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What made each of those three impacts?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: They are the result of a shelling. My balcony was hit by two mortar shells, on two occasions, and considerable part of it was destroyed. But some has been -- something has been repaired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do these three impact points represent three different occasions or less than three occasions of shelling?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: There was shooting and shelling almost every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when --

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: The smaller -- during the day, one didn't dare show up, because you would disappear. Only during the night. That's where we were, that's where we had our meals and watched television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what years or year those three shelling impacts were made?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Well, you know, I had arrived five months prior to the events. I lived in Trnovo. And I managed to escape from there, and I came to live with my daughter. Some of the damage was already there. But the shooting and shelling continued when I arrived. We no longer -- we could no longer take this entrance that you can see. We had pierced an entrance on the other side of the building which we used because we couldn't take the front entrance any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why could you not take the front entrance?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Because it was visible from where the shooting came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that important that it was visible? What would happen if you took the front entrance?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: They would have killed you. Only during the night, when we had to go to fetch water, did we use this entrance to leave the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I ask the witness be shown Photograph 35.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonko, do you recognise what appears in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: It's difficult to recognise this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think in the photograph, one can see a row of apartment buildings slightly to the left of centre and another row --

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- row of apartment buildings slightly to the right of centre, and in between them, one can see an apartment building behind the two front rows. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes, it is. However, the mid part where I lived, there are buildings on both sides, but there is a 10-metre long passage between the buildings which is facing the portion of the front line from where the bullets came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you see any part of your building in this photograph, that is, the building in which you lived on the night you were shot?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to describe that building as it appears in the photograph, or that part of the building?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: You mean only my apartment?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, firstly, the building in which you lived.

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes. This is it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe to us where it is in the photograph, that is, the building in which you lived.

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We cannot see where you are pointing. Can you tell us where it is in the photograph. Perhaps first of all, is it towards the middle of the photograph or to one side of the middle?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Not exactly in the middle, more to the left where entrance number 5 is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, is it possible for the witness in Sarajevo to point to the photograph in a way which can be recorded?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Sarajevo] Yes, Your Honour, we can place the photograph on the ELMO here in Sarajevo, and the witness can point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, would you then please assist the witness in putting the photograph on the Sarajevo ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonko, can you now place your finger or a pointer on the building where you were living on that night and hold the pointer or your finger on that building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask the technical booth or whether we have The Hague ELMO on our screen -- oh, yes, I see the finger of the witness, yes.

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The witness is pointing to a high-rise apartment building in the right portion of the photograph which shows the top layers of the photograph [sic] destroyed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, is that the building in which you were living at the time you were shot?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I ask the witness be shown again Photograph 34A.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonko, I think you see again the photograph that shows you sitting in your apartment, approximately in the position you were in when you were shot. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the background, we can see two buildings and a gap between the two buildings. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any houses between your apartment building and the two buildings we can see in the back of this photograph?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: There were two other buildings where this passage was, and they could see both the right and the left side of this passage. As for the building, there were less impacts on this side, in the shelling. The side -- the building of the other side was also damaged by a shell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Actually, both of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us earlier that from your balcony, it was possible to see an area controlled by the Serb forces, that is, the forces on the other side of the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you could point -- withdraw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: First of all perhaps, Mr. President, Ms. Philpott could place a copy of this photograph on the ELMO in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's 34A.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dzonko, could you please point to any part of the territory held by the Serb forces that you can see in this photograph. Do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes, I do. There was this passage which was situated in between.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, first of all, can you point to the passage between the buildings.

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: That is from this balcony, in this direction, towards the road. Straight ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, could you point to the building which is on the right side of the passage as we look at the photograph.

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which side of the confrontation line was that building on; the Bosnian government side or the other side?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: These buildings were on the Bosnian side. And on the other side of these buildings, there were Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And what about the part that can be seen between the two buildings in that photograph? Which side was that part on?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes. Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Might the witness be shown Photograph 11A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, for the record, we would like to indicate that the witness showed -- pointed to two buildings which he can see from his window, unless there's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I agree with that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Might the witness be shown - I'm sorry - 1A, Photograph 1A.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonko, do you agree with me that this appears to be a close-up taken from your balcony, showing the gap between the two buildings?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Might the witness now be shown 3A.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you now see a further close-up of the gap between the two buildings as seen from your balcony?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Down the bottom of the gap, we can see what appears to be some street lights and a traffic sign. Do you see those?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And immediately behind the street lights, we can see what appears to be a two- or three-storey house with a new roof, perhaps a new house. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes, this building was constructed after the war. The area had been completely destroyed, and there is a new building that was built just recently which was not there at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the confrontation -- where were the confrontation lines in relation to that new building at the time that you were shot?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Exactly on the spot where this new house is. This was their ground. There used to be a house there before, but it was destroyed in shooting. They had a very small house there, which was actually a bunker, and that is where they were shooting from. This area was theirs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the background, one can see a white building with a flat roof, and one can see three rows of windows facing towards your balcony. Do you know what building that was?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: That building is a Catholic monastery. That is where Serbs were. That is where they fired from. And also, it is the faculty of theology.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that is where Serbs fired from, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: They could target everything from there. That is actually where they targeted us from -- that was the most usual spot that they used for targeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that that was the most usual spot used?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Because this is a very large building, and everybody said that that is where they mostly fired from. When -- because the whole area between this little house and further down was under their control.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, would that be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace. Could you give us an indication, just for our planning, on how much time you'd still need for the examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: About 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: About 10 minutes. Mr. Dzonko, we will have a break for half an hour, and then your examination will be continued, first by counsel for the Prosecution, then by counsel for the Defence. We will adjourn until 11.00 local time in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed with the examination-in-chief, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I ask that the witness be shown again photograph 35, from Exhibit P3279T. Perhaps Ms. Philpott could place a copy of the same photograph on the ELMO in Sarajevo as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonko, I show you again a photograph that I showed you earlier. You have explained to us in the meantime that, from your balcony, there was a passage between two buildings of a similar height to yours through which the area on the other side of the confrontation line could be seen.

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the photograph, are you able to see either of the two buildings that were between your apartment and the confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You point to the buildings to the right of the photograph. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Here, in between.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is in between?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: The passageway.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The witness points to the centre of the photograph. Thank you. Might the witness be shown Photograph 076. 076 is the photograph which appears to have some -- yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, just to avoid whatever misunderstanding, usually the last part of the numbering is either numbers or letters, and then not more than two numbers. Could it be 07B?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What appears in that photograph, Mr. Dzonko?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: That's in the corridor, and it is a cupboard, built-in cupboard or whatever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said earlier that the bullet, having left your body, ricocheted off a wall, and ultimately entered a cupboard and hit a chandelier which had been placed in the cupboard for safekeeping. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that cupboard appear in this photograph, or was it a different cupboard?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: It's this cupboard here in the corridor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please point to the particular part of the cupboard that the bullet entered.

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: It hit somewhere here, but I can't actually see it. This upper part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The upper part. Thank you, that will do. Now, when you were discharged from Kosevo Hospital, did you receive any documentation from the hospital staff?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Nothing. I didn't receive anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any stage did you see any documentation -- excuse me for a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. One, with respect to the French translation, and what is going to appear in the transcript. It wasn't what was said by the witness. The reference was to medical documentation and not to anything else. And the other point -- that is my main remark, but the other point is that if we're going to examine this question of documents now that you received a moment ago, I don't know whether it would be convenient to find a way of reading to the witness the pertinent part or the part that is being established. So that is a suggestion on my part. So that is a suggestion on my part, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't hear yet Mr. Ierace asking to present any document to the witness. But if it comes to that, Mr. Ierace, perhaps we would first have a look at the document and see whether it could be done or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonko, at any stage have you received a report apparently from Kosevo Hospital about your injuries and the treatment that you were given at that hospital?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: I didn't receive anything. I received a discharge list, the discharge paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you receive that?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: When I left hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What information did it have on it?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: I didn't actually read it. I put it away somewhere. I don't know where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I ask that Exhibit P2771 be placed on the ELMO. Mr. President, does that meet your requirements?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'd rather first -- if you'd please give it first to the Chamber and give an opportunity to Mr. Piletta-Zanin to give the reasons why he objects against presenting the document to the witness. Yes, if you would please give it just...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you for giving us the floor. What we should like to indicate is the following: That the documenti quasi, totally illegible, except the essential part at the bottom. So what we should like to do is to submit this document directly to the witness, he can read it, and we can see what is to be understood by it. And as I said a moment ago, Mr. President, this portion in the translation, and we have these words here, it says "illegible," and then there's a blank, and then "illegible" and so on. So it's not a document that, reasonably speaking, can be used in this case and in this procedure, and I think it would be far better if the document were to be placed on the ELMO in front of the witness for the witness to read it if he is able to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether it's decisive whether the witness can read it or not, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. But do I understand that it is the position of the Defence that those parts of this document readable could be admitted into evidence and those parts illegible could not be admitted into evidence? Because you asked the witness to read parts of it, which raises this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that there is a reason why -- that there are grounds to reject this document. If you compare the two translations that I handed to you a moment ago - I don't know if you've got them - but those two translations that we received of the documents, one of them is in black and the other one is little clearer, whiter, you will see that it is in fact the same document, which is readable in the upper part, but the English translation is not the same. So this raises an essential problem. We have two documents with two different translations as to the part that is legible. So we cannot accept these documents, and we think that these documents in their entirety, whatever their copies, whether it is the dark copy or the white copy, that they should be rejected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, may I ask you if you present this document to the witness, what is your probative purpose doing so? I can imagine there are many, but please indicate to us what you would like to establish by putting questions to the witness in relation to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, first of all, it corroborates the evidence of the witness as to the date of admission and approximate date of -- and the evidence as to the date of discharge. The witness is identified as the recipient of the treatment by way of his name on the document and his year of birth. The document also contains some information in relation to his diagnosis on discharge, diagnosis on admission, partly, and surgery performed. There is also a reference to him being a wounded person and a reference to a relevant part of his body which is corroborative of the evidence he has given. Mr. President, perhaps I should make the position of the Prosecution clear, because this is related to an ongoing objection. The Prosecution does not say it is necessary for medical records to be tendered before the fact of injury can be established by this Tribunal. That evidence of injury may come from one or more sources. One source, and in my submission, a sufficient source, is a surviving victim informing the Tribunal of the injuries that he received. So in that sense, this document is not essential to the Prosecution case. The Prosecution offers it because it is available and because, to the extent it is legible, it is corroborative of the witness's evidence. But the Prosecution does not lose the evidence of the witness if the document is not tendered. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if you'd like to respond, especially to the position the Prosecution takes in respect of the evidentiary matter raised by the Prosecution, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, willingly. Three points, Mr. President, the first of which is the following: This document is not an original document. The original, as the witness has said, has been put away somewhere by him, by the witness. So that is one problem, the problem of originality of the document. It is not an original. The second point is the eventual probative value of the document. Now, Mr. President, if we look at this last document, which is the version that is most legible, with the one that we received a -- some time ago, we can see that in this document, there are things that were not legible previously. Now, we received this document on the 18th or the 19th, actually - this morning - in our pigeonhole and it is not possible for us to be given documents and exhibits on the same day several hours before the commencement of trial. So that is a matter of principle. The other reason is that the consequence of this is that we should consider this particular document in this particular form as it was presented to us, and it was presented to us just this morning, or maybe last night, which means that the rules concerning the disclosure of documents were not respected. And therefore, this document cannot be received. As to its probative value, I don't know, because I'm not able to read it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I invited you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, also to respond to the position of the Prosecution that the type of injuries we're talking about could be established by other means than medical reports. I'm specifically asking you this because if - I say if - we would exclude this document, apart from the corroboration that might result from it, it would take away for you as well any challenging of the testimony of the witness by using these kind of documents. For example, if a witness would say I have been shot in the left arm, and if a badly legible document would say it would be the right arm, you'd lose an opportunity -- I'm just trying to draw your attention to advantages, and disadvantages, of course, of using these kind of documents. And therefore, I didn't hear any response to Mr. Ierace's remark that he could do without the document as well, and that still the testimony would be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I have a few moments to confer with my colleague? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, for according me those moments to confer. The Defence persists, that is to say, in this state of the document, which is not an original and completely illegible, the Defence does not -- the position of the Defence is that it does not want to have it accepted. We persist in our position. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber feels that it is necessary to shortly deliberate and do it during a short break. Expected we'll be a couple of minutes. We'll adjourn for five minutes or any longer, if necessary. --- Break taken at 11.23 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, before we give a decision on whether it will be admitted or not, the Chamber allows you to present this document to the witness for the obvious first questions. So you may proceed this way. So if the witness could be shown Document P2771. The problem is that I see no witness on my screen. And may I expect that a copy is in Sarajevo, Mr. Ierace? Because it might be a bit difficult to read it from the screen or to...

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't think there is a copy in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No. Perhaps we could try with the screen and see how legible it is.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Sarajevo] It is P2771.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but what I can see from a distance, and may I ask, Mr. Ierace, is the bad legible copy of P2771 in Sarajevo, because it very much looked to me on the screen as the, let's say, the black box.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, you're correct. Excuse me, Mr. President. The document that we have here does not seem to me to be particularly legible on our ELMO, so could I respectfully suggest that the poorer quality document be placed on the ELMO in Sarajevo, and I think it just was. Perhaps it could be placed back on the ELMO in Sarajevo, because the preliminary questions relate to parts of the document which I think are visible on both versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then please put on the ELMO in Sarajevo the -- I would say the bad copy, and the better copy is on the ELMO in The Hague and could be manipulated by zooming in or zooming out. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonko, there is a document placed in the area in front of you. Would you please look at that document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm truly sorry, but I have to say that in respect of the same document, whether we're dealing with the black or the white version, we have received translations emanating from the Office of the Prosecution, and they are not the same. So we have problems of translation. I wanted to draw the Chamber's attention to that fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, we are not yet at a point of the content of the document as far as translation is concerned. When I referred to the obvious questions, I was not looking to any detail of translation. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonko, do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where have you seen it before and when have you seen it before?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Here, ten days ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And before then, had you seen it? In other words, apart from ten days ago, have you seen it before?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: I don't remember. Maybe I've forgotten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Please look closely at the document. And do you see towards the top of the document there is entered your name?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we then please zoom in on the specific spot of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the witness is viewing the poorer quality version in Sarajevo rather than the better quality version here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I'd like him perhaps to look at both.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And perhaps you'll ask him, then, whether he sees the same or any different.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonko, in relation to the copy which is in front of you, do you see that your name appears towards the top part of the document?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: I see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that earlier you told us that you received a discharge paper when you left hospital?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, when did you last see that discharge paper or a copy of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'll withdraw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness has already answered the question. He saw the document ten days ago in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No, that's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please respond, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. In fairness to the Defence, I don't think that I could connect the two at this stage. And I also withdrew the question because I recollected the witness said he had not read the discharge summary. But perhaps I would clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's also my recollection that he said he didn't read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. So again in fairness to the Defence, that's why I withdrew that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonko, would you please look at the top line of the document. Do you see the words "University Medical Centre, Sarajevo"?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see, to the right of those words, "Letter of Discharge"?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I now direct you to the bottom of the document, that is, the bottom left-hand corner. Do you see, in the bottom left-hand corner, some handwriting?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: There's a signature here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there also a date?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise any of the signatures which appear in the bottom left-hand corner of the document?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: There's my signature. The other one, I cannot... That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have some difficulties in following your line of questioning at this moment about dates and --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this stage I'm still directing the witness to the poorer quality copy which he has in Sarajevo. And if you will bear with me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I would first like to instruct Sarajevo. Ms. Philpott.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Sarajevo] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In The Hague, we have two copies of what seems to be the same document. The document the witness has in front of him at this moment, is that a document with a big darkish area, especially on the right side of that document?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Sarajevo] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please put that --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Sarajevo] One has a darker. One copy is darker than the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please put the dark copy... Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Sarajevo] Do you have an ERN number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that it's appearing on our screen. If you put it on the ELMO so that we could compare the ERN numbers. Yes. That copy is now on the ELMO. Could you please move it so that we can see the top of the page. If you would move a bit more downwards. I still cannot see the top of the page. Please -- yes. There is -- am I correct in my understanding, Ms. Philpott, that there's no ERN number on the top of that page?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Sarajevo] That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any other ERN number visible on this very page?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Sarajevo] Yes, Your Honour. The bottom right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please put that on the ELMO. Yes, that's a different... I notice on my screen that at the bottom right-hand corner, I have 0028341, and I think the last number is an 8 as well. Could you confirm that, Ms. Philpott?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Sarajevo] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please leave this document on the ELMO and keep the other copy, for the time being, away from the witness. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonko, you told us that you recognised your signature on the bottom left-hand corner of that document. You also said that you saw there a date. What is the date?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, could you instruct the one who is manipulating the ELMO in Sarajevo to zoom in on the left bottom corner so that we can see it better.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The ELMO is now zooming in, but we are seeing the centre part of the document. Could the document please be manipulated so that the bottom left-hand corner is placed in the middle of the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Sarajevo] I apologise. Your Honour, may I please just say that the document that the witness was first looking at was the other copy, which is bearing a different ERN number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear to us now. This might cause Mr. Ierace to repeat perhaps his last questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, would you be bear with me for a minute, because I think that I observed another document in the possession of Ms. -- of the registrar. The other document, I wonder if that could be placed on the ELMO. The one that is not as dark. And perhaps the camera could be zoomed back. All right. In the top right-hand corner, is there the ERN number 0036-1011?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Sarajevo] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand, Mr. Ierace, that we are now working with a third document of the same document?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It seems that way, Mr. President, and I don't know where the earlier copy came from. The one which is on the screen now is the one I have, which has the darker area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not the one we have. And what copy does Mr. Piletta-Zanin have?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the question, was it in plural or in singular?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, whatever copies you have. We have just been handing out, and I'll just give you the information --
