utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have received --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Piletta-Zanin, we just got 0020-8842, ERN number. We just saw on the screen that, in Sarajevo, there was a very black copy, 0028-3418 ERN number in the down right-hand corner of the document. And there is now a third document with an ERN number, vertical on the right top corner, which I was not able to follow immediately the number, but it ended by 11. Which of these three do you have? Perhaps refer to the last two digits.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll be glad to enlighten the Prosecution. There are only two documents, but three ERN numbers. The document that you consider to be the most legible is the one 0020-8842. This is the document that we received only this morning and the document that we object to. The document that has two ERN numbers, which considerably simplifies things, is the document which we had the opportunity to see a moment ago on the screen, the number being 002 -- I think 3, 44, again I think 3. The copy is so poor that I'm not sure. The document that I submitted to you a moment ago in order to clarify the matters is a document which bears also another number. You will see it on the document. There's the first number and the second number, which is 0036-1010. So we have two documents, one of them having two numbers, only one of the numbers being legible. And another one with a third number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't think that it matters that there are versions which have different ERN numbers. The explanation for the ERN number which appears in the top right-hand corner of the copy on the ELMO at the moment is that it was attached to a statement by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And it consecutively followed on from the ERN numbers of that statement. In that statement -- perhaps I should leave it at that in the presence of the witness, Mr. President. My basic point is I don't think its of any consequence, and perhaps if I could continue with the questioning I could take the witness to the relevant issue and perhaps give an explanation later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I'd like to know for certain what document you're using when putting questions to the witness. Because I thought it would be the clearer copy, and it then turned out, when I had difficulties in following your line of questioning, especially on the left bottom part of the dates and signatures, I had difficulties in following your questioning. So therefore, I would say that you have to be quite clear on what document you're using and provide the Chamber with that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we can turn off the witness's ability to hear what I'm about to say, I can give you a very brief explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask -- first of all, indicate to the Registry in Sarajevo that we might turn off the sound for you in a moment in order to discuss legal technical matters that have been raised, and we'll be in touch with you again soon. May I then ask whether it's possible - I'm asking this to the technical booth - to --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Sarajevo] Your Honour, I have removed the headset from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If that -- when the headset is removed, Ms. Philpott, could you confirm to us that without the headset, you cannot hear what words are spoken in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Sarajevo] Yes, that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we still have the picture on our screen of Sarajevo. We can see that the witness is not wearing at this moment a headset. Then please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, firstly to put this issue in its proper perspective, what we're dealing with is simply a letter of discharge in relation to this witness. Nothing more than that. The witness made a statement to an investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor on the 13th of November, 1995. And I anticipate that the witness will give evidence that the date which appears above his signature in the bottom left-hand corner of the copy in front of him, is the 13th of November. In other words, he signed it on the occasion of him making a statement to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My problem, Mr. Ierace, is that I have a copy in front of me which bears, in the left bottom corner, not something that seems to be the signature of the witness, nor a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'm coming to that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, you will remember I earlier said that there was a mission to Sarajevo to obtain more legible copies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- of medical reports. The legible or more legible version that you have is a product of that mission. One would not expect the copy held by the hospital to have the signature of the -- of this witness and the date, because, of course, he made that on a copy which was retained by the Office of the Prosecutor. That's why I'm taking him to these particulars on the poorer quality version, simply to link him to the letter of discharge. We then go from the poor quality one, having established that link, to the better quality one. But my overall point is that it has taken us a lot of time, and really what this really comes down to is simply linking him to this document, which in any event carries legibly his name, the nature of the document, and his date of admission. So perhaps I could, in a short form, accelerate this process and leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You -- yes, but whatever -- I'm not saying that you would not be allowed to do so, Mr. Ierace. If you are putting questions to the witness on the basis of a bad quality, even if it's just in order to link him to the better legible copy, we would like to be able to follow your questions and what the witness's answers are and to see whether we can with our own eyes see that if you're asking about a date, that there is a date on that document. And we don't have a copy. Do you have any copies of the -- I mean, even if you would tender both the bad and the good copy, just in order to...

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I apologise for that, Mr. President. I thought that all of the poorer quality ones, that is the ones which had the black area, carried the signature and the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The better -- yes, the poorer one. But we didn't have the poorer one. We returned it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we just have the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I understand how the confusion came about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we just keep the copy for a second so that we can follow your questioning. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps Ms. Philpott could arrange for the witness's headphones to be replaced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Perhaps wait for one second, Ms. Philpott. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with your permission, I should like to intervene in response to what Mr. Ierace has just indicated. First of all, because we cannot verify whether the system is working, the ERN number that Mr. Ierace stated, the one that we can read on the second document, I should like Mr. Ierace to read it out so that we know exactly what number we are talking about. If I understand the issue correctly, the witness was asked to sign a document of this kind, that is, a document which was totally illegible. And thirdly, the reason why we have been asking for original documents is simply because, if we're going to have to work with two copies, with three numbers, it is going to be very difficult. The originals simplify things, and we believe that they should be found somewhere, as we have seen in the case of Witness Besic, the other day. Let us not waste any more time. Let us have this cleared up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the Prosecution is not able to at this very moment, if I do understand them well, to produce the original copy of this -- the original of this document. And we all are aware there are two different copies, one I would say the black box, and the other one major parts illegible. The black-box one appears to have a signature and a date on it. The other one has not. And for the time being, we'll proceed on the basis of these copies available to the Prosecution, to the Defence, and to the Chamber. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness could have his headphones back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonko, would you please look at the bottom left-hand corner of the document that you looked at earlier. For the record, that is Exhibit P2771.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Sarajevo] May I have the ERN number, please, Mr. Ierace, just to be sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you're creating problems, Mr. Ierace. You said 2771, but that's, of course, the well-legible copy, and the other copies, as far as I can see, have no numbers on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So let me just perhaps assist you in instructing the Registry in Sarajevo to put on the ELMO a document which has in the right top corner, but vertically, the ERN number 0036-1011.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Sarajevo] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Again, I would ask that the ELMO zoom in on the bottom left-hand corner. Thank you. Yes. If you can just stop there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonko, what is the date -- first of all, can you point to your signature, please, on the document.

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the date which appears on the document near your signature?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: The 13th of November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that your writing?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many statements have you made to investigators of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. For the transcript, the witness placed his picture in between three signatures, one which is ascendant and clear, and the other is lower down. Now, for the purposes of the transcript, for the record, may we describe exactly the position in which the witness indicated that his signature was to be located.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just do it briefly. The witness pointed at a signature on the same height as 13-11. That's the second box from above, left-hand side, at the left bottom corner of the document. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I withdraw the earlier question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonko, do you remember when you placed your signature on that document?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: [No Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonko, do you remember when you placed your signature on that document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, but the French translation and at the bottom of the transcript, we have another signature. I am very sorry. But could this be put right in the French transcript. Thank you in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I cannot see the French transcript, but may I ask specific attention for the preparation of the French transcript, if necessary even to listen to what has been originally said, and that it appears properly in the French transcript. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonko, I apologise, we did not hear your answer. I will ask the question again. Do you remember when you placed your signature on this document?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: I can't remember when it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times have you given or signed a statement for investigators of the Tribunal's Prosecution office?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: I don't know that either. Whenever I went, I would sign.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what year did you first sign a statement for an investigator from the Prosecutor at the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: I can't remember that either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whenever that was, did you give any papers to the investigator?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: No, I didn't. No papers of any kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now that you have looked at the document in front of you for a longer period of time, I ask you this question: Apart from ten days ago, do you remember having seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm very sorry, but as we presented two documents with different numbers and showed them to the witness, could Mr. Ierace say what document he's referring to now. Could he specify, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could you please do so, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm referring to the document on which the witness has identified his signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonko, do you remember -- I withdraw the last question. Do you remember why you signed this document?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Well, what shall I say? I signed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please -- I'll ask the question again. Do you remember why you signed this document? In other words, what the reason was that you signed it, and also, I should add, placed the date of the 13th of November on it?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I can't remember why.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I won't take that issue any further.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonko, you have earlier pointed out to us from photographs an area which was controlled by Serb forces on the occasion that you were shot. What part of Sarajevo is that, that is, the area controlled by Serb forces which you could see through the gap between the buildings?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: It's called Nedzarici. That's it. And then Stupsko Brdo is down there. And then the Lukavica road continues on down there. But where the building is, that is Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I ask the witness be shown again on our ELMO here and on the ELMO in Sarajevo photograph 35 from Exhibit 3279T.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonko, earlier you identified the gap between the two buildings that stood between your apartment and the Serb-controlled area. You identified the gap as appearing, in this photograph, towards the centre of the photograph. In relation to the buildings on either side of the gap, in mid-1994, that is, around the time you were shot, did anyone live in those buildings, that is, the buildings on either side of the gap and in front of your apartment?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes. In front of our apartment, there was another building, but nobody lived on that side of the building, just the side of the building that our building was on. We weren't allowed to look at that passageway, but to the left and right of the passageway, it was free because it was protected by this building. So it was only where I lived that you could see right down there between -- in the space between the two buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Now, you've told us about the difficulties you had in entering and departing your building from the front entrance. I think you said you used the front entrance only at night to find water --

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- to collect water.

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you left the building, other than nighttime, did you walk on the surface or in some other means? Did you cross ground by some other means?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Well, during the daytime [as interpreted], we would get through on the opposite side. They broke down one apartment, and we could go that way. But during the daytime, we didn't dare go out. We didn't dare go into this passage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Clearly on the night you were shot you had access to electricity because you told us the television was on. Were there times in 1993 and 1994 when you did not have power?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Well, there wasn't any electric power all the time, just when it was this world football championships. That's when they let us have some electricity for a day or two, and that was the last day of those football matches. It was the world championship, so we had electricity then, but otherwise, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you -- I withdraw that. Did your apartment have an elevator, that is, your apartment block?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you get water up to your apartment when there was no power?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: We used the stairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there times when you took shelter elsewhere in the apartment block from fire, in particular, shelling?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Well, you could only go through the other side, the -- from the other room where it was protected. Because otherwise, there could be a stray bullet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ierace. May I just ask you whether you'd -- these documents, are you going finally to tender any or all of them in evidence? So I think it's good to know before we start the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I will seek to tender them on the basis that the witness has said he received a letter of discharge from the hospital when he left. The document speaks for itself. It identifies the witness, his year of birth, his date of admission, the name of the hospital, and the nature of the document, all of which are consistent with the witness's evidence. The witness identifies his signature on a photocopy of the document, although he no longer recollects why he placed his signature there or when he placed it there or what the purpose of the signature on the document was. The more legible copy is admissible on the basis that a comparison with the less legible copy reveals it to be the same document, but in a more legible form. Having regard to my earlier observations as to the relevance of this material, while I say it is admissible and it is of assistance to the Trial Chamber, I simply make clear that I take the view that it does not diminish -- if it is not accepted into evidence, the evidence of the witness is not diminished by that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't hear you refer to the diagnosis parts, neither on the top or on the bottom. Would you seek to rely on that as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Even on the more legible version, little of the diagnosis part is comprehensible. When one has regard to the translation of that bottom part into the English language, it's only every occasional word that is decipherable. There are references to body parts in decipherable words which are consistent with the area of injury, but I appreciate that that's as far as it goes. It may be that the Trial Chamber takes the view that part of the document is not admissible, and I accept that, clearly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, is the Defence ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we will be ready, but before we go ahead - and thank you for asking - I would just like to remind you of the fact that the Defence is categorically opposed to admittance into evidence of the two documents, both of them, the one that the witness had in his hand, and the other because, for the moment, Mr. Ierace is tendering one. That's the first point. The second point is that we are opposed to it all the more so as the only thing that we can see is the witness was visited by a gynecologist. Now, this is a little troubling. We see that at the bottom, the doctor is a gynecologist, which is a little disquieting. So we're not certain what happened to this witness, and as to the diagnosis, it is essential to have one. So until we have these two documents, it would be blinding to justice and the Defence, so -- and it would mislead us. So do you want us to commence the cross-examination now, Mr. President? What I wanted to know really was whether the documents are admitted into evidence or not, in light of what you said a moment ago. If they are not admitted, then the position of the Defence is clear. If they are admitted, we shall have to accept it. But we would like to hear the ruling before we go ahead with the cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you asked for a decision. Of course, you could -- if we give a decision now, we do not know whatever will come up during cross-examination so it would be a provisional decision to that extent. Of course, we are not on a jury trial here where you keep away from a jury a document or not. Let me first tell you that it's the understanding of the Chamber that Mr. Ierace tenders both the signed copy and the best legible copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I think that there's some misunderstanding as far as what will be tendered. The provisional decision of this Chamber is that the form as such, especially the upper part, let's say, where it comes from and even some of the stamps, are clearly legible, that the diagnosis part, especially the middle part, is not legible. But just to give you an example, the name of the witness appears quite clear on the document; the date of birth, just the year, is quite legible; the date of admission is quite legible, and the date of discharge also seems to be quite legible. So this Chamber provisionally decides that this document or these documents are admissible in evidence, but only to the limited purpose of establishing from the upper part, which is clearly legible in its content, in its context, and I gave you a few examples of that just a minute ago, so if this is of guidance when cross-examining the witness, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your ruling, Mr. President. May I now address - or do I do it through you, Mr. President - Ms. Philpott, who was standing next to the witness in Sarajevo? May I address her directly, speak to her directly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you give her instructions, you may do it directly in order to save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Ms. Philpott, I know that you're well able to follow French, and this will be in French, so would you please place on the ELMO next to the witness Document Number ERN 0020-8842, please. It is the document which is the clearer of the two copies, I think. And it also has a provisional number, P for Prosecution, 2771. 2771, P.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Sarajevo] I'm sorry, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I do not have a document with that ERN number.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President [In English] Not a problem. Thank you very much for this information indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would please have it...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we are going to have to work with the exhibit on the screen. But in the meantime, let me say good morning to the witness. Cross-examined by Mr. Piletta-Zanin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me, Witness?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: I can hear you, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, we are now going to enable you to see something on your screen. It is a document that has just appeared on our own screens. Can you see the document, too, Witness?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: I can, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it a document with the following number at the top, and that number is 20-8842. Is that the number of the document?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: I can't see it very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Witness, would you now please point, with your finger, to the square where it says in the Serbian language, I think, the date of discharge, the date you left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the document is on The Hague ELMO where the witness is not able to point at.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I know. But I thought we could ask Ms. Philpott to indicate this to the witness. But I'll proceed in a different way. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you see on the document you have before you, in the central part of the first square, a rectangle in the first box where it says, in Serbian, the word "Filijala"?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: I can't say see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Witness, now could you count eight boxes down the page, on the left-hand side, from top to bottom, and stop yourself in the eighth box or rectangle, moving from top to bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, wouldn't it be a good idea to zoom in specifically on those parts you'd like to show to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can zoom in, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you now see the box, the space in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: I can see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you see a first date?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: I can see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you read it out, please, Witness. If you cannot, then tell us.

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: I can't see it very well. There's a 1. I can see a 1. I can't see it well enough.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You're not able to read the year either, are you?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Witness. Would you now read out, Witness, please, what it says, that is to say, the first digit in Arabic letters in the inferior part, right below, and we've zoomed in on it. Could you read what the first digit is down below that.

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: I can't see it well enough.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Witness, I'm now going to ask the technical booth to zoom in to the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zoom right, please. Thank you, a little bit more. Move right. Thank you. Stop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, it says -- you have here a box, a rectangular one, and there's a printed inscription inside. Can you see that box with the printed letters? The first word is "Adresa." Can you see where it says "Adresa" typed in?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: You mean in the middle here?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that's it. Witness, as you can see it --

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: It says "Mjesto." "Mjesto" and the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, underneath that box where you've just read out the word "Mjesto," there's another box, and then a third box with some typing, some typewritten words in it. Can you see that third box?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: "Adresa," you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Now, Witness, would you please read out, loud and clear, the words that have been typed in in that box.

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Well, I haven't got my glasses with me, and I can't read it. I can't see well enough to read.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when you came to this examination, didn't you think that you would probably have documents to read?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nobody told you that if you cannot see very well --

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: I have problems with my sight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you have your glasses with you?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when you signed your statement, did you have your glasses?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when you signed this document in this obscure version, did you have your glasses with you?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, at the time you signed this document, were you asked to read this document before signing it?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: They read it out to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you verify -- so they asked you to read this obscure document, the one that you have in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, the document that you signed is the document that was read out to you.

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was it? What do you mean when you say "they"?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that "they" had read it out to you. Who do you have in mind? Who did you mean when you said "they"?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: My daughter was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when you say "they," "they came," who do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: My daughter was here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I understand that your daughter was there. But apart from your daughter, the individuals who read the document out to you, who were they?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: The people who were here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But who were they?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that my friend indicate to the witness what he means by the words "the document."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you have referred to different documents while questioning before. You referred to the statement of the witness, you referred to other documents as well. Would you please be very clear in when you're talking about a document. But apart from that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [In English] Absolutely sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I think since we interrupted the cross-examination anyhow, it's time for a break of 20 minutes. Mr. Dzonko, we'll have a break for 20 minutes, and then we'll continue. So we'll adjourn until 5 minutes to 1.00 local time in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just before my learned colleague resumes his cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, one moment, please. I saw that General Galic was not yet in the courtroom. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Before my learned colleague resumes his cross-examination, I seek to inform the Trial Chamber that the Defence and Prosecution have agreed to a change in the order of the videolink witnesses. Instead of Fatima Pita following Marko Kapetanovic and Ramiza Kundo, Fatima Pita will now follow Kapetanovic. Mr. President, it's also clear, I think, that we are unlikely to finish the videolink witnesses by Thursday. Perhaps it would be prudent to inquire as to whether we could extend into Friday with videolink. The reason for the change is that Mr. Mundis will be taking Fatima Pita, and he is not available after tomorrow. If Fatima Pita is not concluded by tomorrow, then I will, with the leave of the Trial Chamber, take over the relevant part of the Prosecutor's role in relation to her evidence from Thursday morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Ierace, for informing the Chamber. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you hear me once again?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, let me go back to the document which you had on your -- on the screen a moment ago. That is the document bearing the number P2771. If necessary, we can perhaps ask at the same time that it be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, the document that you see here, the one that you have in your hand and which was submitted to the witness, the one with the signatures. Thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness - yes, we can perfectly see it now. Thank you. Witness, can you see this document in front of you? I think that you --

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you have it in the other version as well. You said a moment ago that they had read it out to you. Who did you have in mind when you said "they"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this gets back to the objection I made just before the break when I asked that Mr. Piletta-Zanin clarify first which document he was referring to, because he referred to statements as well as the medical discharge summary. And the question he has just asked makes a presumption in that regard. I ask that he first clarifies with the witness which document was read to him, whether it was this document or his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please do so, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll be happy to do that, Mr. President. Now we are talking about the document that I had put on the ELMO, and the references of which I have just provided.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, with respect to this document, the one which is in front of you and which you can see on the screen, whose number is P2771, did you state the following: "They read it out to me"? That is my first question.

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: When I was here, a woman read the document for me because I have -- I read with difficulty generally speaking, so I couldn't make out everything that was written on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you are telling me now that you signed the document, but that you did not read it. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: I asked her to read it out for me because I couldn't see it very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when you signed this document, the document was read out to you. Was that the case?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like to know whether the entire document was read out to you.

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did they also read the entire diagnosis, which can be found at the bottom of the document?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Which diagnosis? Of my wound? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, in all likelihood in relation to the wound that you had sustained.

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, at the time, were you able to understand the diagnosis as it was read out to you?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, am I correct in understanding that the document was read out to you, and that the reading of the document was comprehensible? Was that the case?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, the person or the persons who had read out this document, did they have any other document with them in their hands?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they only had this document, the one that we are currently discussing, P2771?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that document of the same quality as the one that you now have in front of you and that you can see on the screen?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes, what we saw just a moment ago on the screen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the document that is now on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the document be zoomed out so that we have a --

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for your assistance, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, we are talking about this particular document. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answer. Since you told us that everything was comprehensible, that is, the text that you were shown, I should now like the technicians to move down to the bottom left side, the bottom left box of the document, if it is possible. And to focus, to zoom in --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [In English] We would like to have zoom on the left corner. Yeah, correct. Thank you very much indeed. Stop here, please. Stop here, please. That will be right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, can you read the text which is written under the first signature, the first one which we can see under this box? There is the first signature which spills over to the adjacent box, and will you please read out for us the text that you can see underneath.

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: You mean where my signature is?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I cannot see what you're pointing at, Witness. But there is a signature in this box that you can see. There is a very big first letter which sort of leans towards right, and there is a typed-out text underneath. Can you please read that text for us?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: I can see the text, but I cannot read it. I cannot make it out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time you signed this document, you didn't have your glasses with you. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you now read out for us the text that is written under this large signature?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: The 13th of November, my name and surname; Dzonko Rasid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Were you ever examined by a gynecologist? And I apologise for the question.

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: At the hospital?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever been examined by a gynecologist? In hospital, yes.

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: There were several physicians. I don't know what they were specialised in. There were several of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know whether the physician who examined you was a gynecologist or not?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answer. Let me move on to a different subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, for one and simple reason, because we are not able to read what is contained in this document, we cannot see whether this document is signed by a gynecologist really concerns this patient. It is the quality of the document that is hampering my intentions in this respect.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the question. We didn't get it.

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Here in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The interpreter in the English language indicated that she did not get Mr. Piletta-Zanin's question. And therefore, we have an answer in response to no question. So perhaps he could repeat the question for the benefit of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was following the French channel, so I didn't notice that the transcript says that the question should be repeated. Please, would you do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I was going to -- I was about to ask the Prosecution to follow the French channel. But I'll be happy to repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you confirm that you did give a written statement in Sarajevo. Can you confirm that for us?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot remember when that was. I don't know. It was years ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm not interested in the date; I'm just interested in your giving the statement. Do you remember giving a statement?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when the OTP investigators came to videorecord your apartment, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when that was?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: I don't know. I have forgotten that, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time of the year was it?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: For the statement? I don't know. I don't know which year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm talking about the videotape, the film in which you figure. When was that filmed; in what period of the year?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Last year, sometime in the spring.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did they ask you at that time to confirm your previous statements?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, a moment ago, you read us a date, the 13th of November. Is that correct? Was that date on the document that you saw on the screen? Can you confirm that, please.

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: You mean what I signed?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Quite correct. Can you confirm what you just said?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: I don't know what. What do you want me to confirm?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take your time, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please help us [In English] We need to have the same document on the ELMO. [Interpretation] Yes, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I can now see the document. A moment ago, you read a date, the 13th of November, and your name next to it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please go on.

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: But I don't know which year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. In response to a question put to you by the Prosecutor, you stated some time ago that you had seen the document ten days ago. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, can you explain to us, how is it possible that we have the date of the 13th of November, whatever the year was, whereas today is the 19th of March, how is it possible that you saw a document of this kind only ten days ago?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: I just signed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, the date that you can see on the document, the 13th of November, the document in respect of which you say that you saw it only ten days ago, was this also written in your hand?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, since we have a very important problem with the dates, is it possible that someone asked you to write down this date here?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Witness, I'm going to help you. Do you know whether in the course of the month of November 1994, 9-4, 1994, that you gave a statement at the OTP -- for the OTP?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: It's possible, because I don't know how many times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Witness, you said a moment ago that you lived in the area of Trnovo, the district of Trnovo. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes, I lived in Trnovo, and I live in Sarajevo now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for specifying. You said that you left Trnovo at the beginning of the conflict. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, do you know if at the beginning of the conflict, and to be more specific, towards July and August 1992, 9-2, important fighting took place in Trnovo between at least two factions that were there? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, thank you for your answer. Now, is it true, on the other hand, that Trnovo was bombed by both of the two camps during the fighting?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Well, there was shelling, and we had to flee from the shelling. But our side didn't have any weapons, and they didn't do the shelling. They targeted us from up above, targeted our houses, from tanks and mortars, Howitzers, for three days and three nights, and we had to flee. We had to escape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Now, Witness, isn't it true that the Muslim forces recaptured Trnovo?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Two months later, two months after that, the Muslims took over, took control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Would I be right in saying that in the region, important fighting took place throughout this time? There was a lot of fighting; would that be true?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Well, yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for your answer. Let me now move on to another question pertaining to your family. You said that when you were wounded, three of your daughters were with you or were living with you in the Sarajevo apartment. Could you tell us, please, the names - first and last names - of those three individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't think that's the evidence, that is, that his three daughters were living with him in that apartment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please, then, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, specify.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I will specify. I don't know if the witness can hear what I'm saying now - this is a slight technical problem - but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you just guide us to the spot where it is in the testimony, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to have to take a little time in order to do so, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you help us, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. Page 14, line 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you found it, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just looking for it. Yes, I can see that the witness actually said that he was at that moment with his three daughters in the apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And also page 19, line 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see the problem. I just wanted to ask the witness to confirm that he had three daughters, and that he would give us the names of those three daughters, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, then it must be a translation problem. I think you're referring to the three daughters living with the witness, of which you'd like to have the name. Let me just check. Your question was: "You said that when you were wounded, three of your daughters were with you or were living with you in the Sarajevo apartment. Could you tell us, please, the names." So you are implying that they might have been with him or might have been living with him. And I think the objection of Mr. Ierace is that the testimony was just that they were with him and not were living with him. I don't think it's a -- unless it turns out to be a major problem, so let's not spend too much time on it. Could you please rephrase your question and continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when you were wounded, you were with your three daughters. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, is it correct that at the time you were living with at least one of your daughters? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give us her name, her full name, please.

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Mediha Gojo [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm checking the transcript, Mr. President. I think the name is Golo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you repeat it for the transcript, Witness. Could you repeat the surname. Is it Golo?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes, Golo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the English transcript, the name is Golo, G-O-L-O.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, let me go back to what your daughter could have said in a statement, but I'll come back to that later. Now I'd like to concentrate on your own statement. You said that you were living at the time about 50 metres from the front line. Is that right? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, how was this front line apparent? That is to say, what did it consist of? What were the material facets of the front line physically?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Well, we didn't dare go there. We just kept to this side. I never actually saw it. All I knew was that shooting was coming from that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Witness. So you were living in that apartment throughout, shall we say, the autumn of 1992 and to the end of the summer of 1994. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time, perhaps even at night, did you see the front line physically, which was 50 metres from your apartment, or not?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: No, I didn't see anything. I only saw once when the liberation came and when peace was signed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's go back to the liberation time. Where and how was the front line built up which was 50 metres from your apartment, as you said?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: I don't know. There was some sort of bunkers there, and the army was in those -- the soldiers were in those bunkers. Several houses, this row of houses, that was the front line, the enemy front line. And I can say that because I saw it when we dared go there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for the answer. Now, you said "houses." Witness, were they residential houses?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, let me repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned houses that made up the front line. Were they residential homes, residential houses, Witness?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes, residential, but that's where the army was. There were no civilians there. So this was the border, the line, the front line, and that belonged to the army, the army held it. And there were bunkers in those houses, several of the house were destroyed and there were bunkers there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, I think I'm going to need your assistance once again. Could we please place on the ELMO a photograph numbered 35. It's the same number, the 0012-12/35. That's the end number. The end digits are 3-5.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you're going to see a photograph. Let me check it. Yes, that's the right one. It's on the screen. Can you see the photograph in front of you, Witness?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. On the right-hand side of the buildings, on the right-hand side of the photograph, there are some buildings, and they seem to be considerably damaged.

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now the highest point above those buildings seems to be in a worse situation than the others. Now, you told us a moment ago, Witness, that there was a residential block which is where the army was. Was it these blocks here? Are those the blocks?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: No, the small buildings. I mean the small buildings by the passageway between the buildings. But on the right-hand side, that was the -- damaged most, and it was through that passageway -- it was that passageway that they targeted most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was listening to what you were saying in Serbian, and you said that the army, the soldiers were in the passageway somewhere, that you indicated to us a moment ago. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Whose army? Whose soldiers?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Serb. The Serb soldiers. It's up to you to say, Witness. It's up to you to tell me, Witness.

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Well, in the passageway and down where the small private houses were, that was where the Serb army was, where the Serb soldiers were, whereas in these buildings here, they weren't there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, who was opposite the Serbian army in the passage?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace. One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: There are a number of confusing elements that have emerged in the last page, at least one of them, according to the English transcription, is a result of a proposition being put to the witness on the basis that he had said it earlier, and in the English translation he hadn't. We now have a situation in relation to the passage, something about soldiers in the passageway. I anticipate that there is confusion in the mind of the witness in relation to what is meant by "the passageway," in other words, whether it refers to the actual passageway or what can be seen through the passageway. And I'd be grateful if that can be clarified with the witness so as to avoid further confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please do so, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, gladly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when you were speaking about the passage, what did you mean? What passage? What were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Well, the passageway between the two lines of buildings, but nobody went that way during the war. Nobody went out onto that passage, and all the residents, the tenants, in those high-rise buildings, they were turned the opposite side. But nobody could live down there, nor did they, and it has all been destroyed. They only lived this side. On both sides of the passage, but nobody went down that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's get things straight. I know what you mean, but it might not be clear to everybody. On the screen, we have a photograph which is 1A, the last digit is 1, and the letter is A. 1A.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, could you place that photograph from the set on the ELMO and we'll go back to that one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now Witness, can you see this new photograph on the screen with that number? Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, then, Witness, would it be correct to say that this passage that we can see between the railings of your balcony is the passage that you were talking about a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, we can take that photo off the screen now, please, and leave the second one there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, the passage that we can see between the two blocks of buildings, the blocks of high-rise buildings, it is roughly in the centre of the photograph. Now, that same passage, it is that same passage but taken from the opposite side. Is that right? From --

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: That's right, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that everything has become clear now for one and all. A moment ago you said that it was in that passageway which is opposite your balcony, or rather, that you can see from your balcony, that there were soldiers. Now, which soldiers were you referring to? Which soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Where the two-storey buildings were, they were Serb soldiers, where the smaller houses were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, opposite them, if there were soldiers, whose soldiers would they be? Which soldiers would those be?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. The Serb army was down there. Who was there? There were bunkers. You couldn't see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when you speak about people in the bunkers, do you mean the Sarajevo army? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: No. No. They couldn't be that army there. I don't know where it was, but it wasn't there. I have no idea where they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, who were the people in the bunkers, then, that you mentioned? Who were they?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: The Serb army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, my question, Witness, is the following: Opposite the army that you said was the Serb army, who was there opposite the Serb army?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Well, the buildings. There was nobody, just the buildings. They were opposite them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were no soldiers, Witness? Were there no soldiers opposite the Serb army?

utterances.speaker: RASID DZONKO
utterances.text: Possibly there were. I don't know. I wasn't interested where they were or where our army was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you never saw any Bosnian soldiers as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you now have put, I think, the same question in different forms five, six times, to the witness. I think the witness is not in a position to give any further answer. So please proceed with some other question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Now, Mr. President, am I authorised to read the written statement of this witness out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if that's relevant. Of course it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, before I go on to my next question, your answer to me several times was no. Now, I'm going to read out a passage from the statement that you gave on the 13th of November, 1994, and I'm going to say that the ERN number is 0103-9375. The text that I have in front of me is in English, and states the following: [In English] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting. Before my learned friend reads that, the date of the statement is in fact the 13th of November, 1995, not 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will give you the text, and you can read the number. I read out 4, and at school I was taught that this was a 4, but I can provide you with the document and the Trial Chamber can read the date for themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, Mr. Piletta-Zanin is quite insisting on his year and you're on yours. Is there something we have to decide, or...?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I can provide you with the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if necessary, we'll ask you to provide it to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps it could come via me, Mr. President. That might shorten this dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please first show it to Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think I see the confusion. If this is the document my friend was about to read from, that is, in fact, a statement dated the 29th of August, 2000. He starts off by saying: "Further to my previous statement dated 13 November, 1994..." But when one goes to that statement, one sees in fact that it was the 13th of November, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, do we understand that you're reading from a statement given in a November month or in an August month?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm going to read the text that I have, which makes reference to the first statement of the 13th of November, 1994, and the statement that seems to have been taken on the 29th of August, 2000, and recognised by the witness. And then I'm going to read out part of the statement dated the 13th of November, 1994. But I'll start off with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, your answer is that you're reading now from the August statement. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, on the 29th of August, 2000, you said the following, and I'm going to quote: [In English] "I would say that all of the Bosnian soldiers that I saw were infantrymen." [Interpretation] Witness, you've just told me that you didn't see any soldiers belonging to the Bosniak army. How come, then, that you stated it would appear the opposite on the 29th of August, 2000, referring to your statement of the 13th of November, 1994?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonko, did you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you understand the question put to you by Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me try to see whether I could phrase the question so that we get an answer from you. Mr. Dzonko, I do understand that you identified in one of your earlier statements the Bosnian soldiers as being infantrymen. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please tell us where and when you saw these Bosnian soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From time to time, I might see them when they pass by. They had a kitchen somewhere in another building. I didn't see it, I never went to that kitchen, but I would see them sometimes, two or three of them, going to have breakfast or lunch when there was a lull in the shooting, when there was no shooting. But I didn't actually like looking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever see them in a position opposite to where you told us the Serbian soldiers were, close to the passageway you just described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, I don't know which way they went.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, we are close to a quarter to 2.00. Could you indicate to us how much more time you'd need for the cross-examination so in order to give --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I please confer with my colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, Mr. President, at least one more hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will then check during the break on how much time is still available for you. I'll do some bookkeeping but not do it now right away. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, two issues: Firstly, if the witness is to be sent away, would you think it appropriate to ask him to come tomorrow with his glasses? And secondly, is it a break that's coming up or the end of the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I would say a break to adjourn until tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, in that event, I'd be grateful if you could suggest to the witness he bring his glasses tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Dzonko, we have not yet finished your examination. Would it be possible for you to return tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I haven't got any glasses, and I can't see with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonko, that would be my second question, that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. if you would return tomorrow morning to the same place, could you bring your glasses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do I need them for? I don't know anything anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, as you may have noticed, sometimes either the Prosecution or the Defence asks you to read something; and without glasses, it's extremely difficult. And we hope it is better with glasses. So would you please be so kind to bring your glasses tomorrow. We'll see for what purpose they are needed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can only read one letter at a time, one by one, and it takes me a long time to make up a word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that. And of course, if the glasses will not help you, we'll then see what to do. But would you be willing to bring your glasses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can bring them, but it will be the same as it is now. It will be no different than it is now. There is nothing that can be different. I would do it willingly if I could, if I knew how, but I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I don't expect you to read any better right away, but if you bring your glasses, perhaps for looking at the pictures on the screen, or for whatever reasons, it's always handy to have them with you. Would you please bring them? I didn't hear your answer. I saw you speaking, but I didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if I can come tomorrow. I'm not a well man. My health isn't good. I don't know if I'll be able to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps if you take a rest this afternoon, and I'm certain that you'll get the necessary assistance to come. It will not presumably take more than one hour tomorrow. So would you please come back tomorrow morning if your health allows you to do so. And I'm certain that the Registry available in Sarajevo will be of your assistance to come.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much in advance, Mr. Dzonko. You'll be excused for now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there anything else to be discussed at this very moment? If not, we'll adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00, in this same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 1.50 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 20th day of March, 2002, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
